Iran’s supreme leader urges Guards-linked Basij volunteers to broaden social reach

RBI buys no gold for six months but brings another 60 tonnes home
body: For gold, the RBI's pause matters more than the repatriation. Central bank buying has been one of the pillars of the long rally, and a year without additions from one of the biggest official buyers weakens that support just as prices struggle to find a floor. Moving gold home doesn't affect global supply or demand, though it does underline the trend among central banks of keeping reserves within their own borders. A return to buying by the RBI would be a meaningful positive for sentiment. The rupee is likely to dictate the timing, since the central bank has prioritised currency stability. Future monthly reserve data will show whether buying resumes.

India's central bank has added virtually no gold in a year, holding steady at 880 tonnes, but it keeps bringing its bullion home, with about 84% now stored in India as falling prices shrink gold's share of reserves.

The Reserve Bank of India bought no gold in the six months to the end of September, but it kept bringing its existing bullion home, shifting around 60 tonnes from overseas vaults to domestic storage, according to its latest half-yearly report on foreign exchange reserves (dated November 25).

The RBI held 880.52 tonnes of gold at the end of September, exactly the same as at the end of March and virtually unchanged from a year earlier. Of that total, 740.13 tonnes were held in India, while 140.39 tonnes were in safe custody with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements. Six months earlier, about 680 tonnes were stored domestically and close to 198 tonnes abroad, with a further 2.8 tonnes held as gold deposits.

Based on calculations from the RBI's data, roughly 84% of India's gold reserves now sit at home, up from about 77% at the end of March. In March 2024, less than half was held domestically. The central bank brought home around 168 tonnes in the 2025/26 fiscal year alone, after moving just over 100 tonnes in each of the two previous years.

The repatriation changes where the gold is kept, not how much the RBI owns, so it adds nothing to demand for the metal. The more telling signal for gold markets is the absence of fresh buying. India was among the steady central bank buyers that helped drive gold's long rally. A pause by a buyer of its size takes away one source of support at a time when prices are already under pressure.

The value of the RBI's gold fell to about $106 billion at the end of September from around $115 billion in March, cutting gold's share of India's total foreign exchange reserves to about 14.4% from 16.7%. Prices drove the decline. The RBI said gold averaged about $4,721 an ounce in April and around $4,319 in September, a drop of roughly 9%, as rising US Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy outweighed safe-haven demand.

The pause also fits the RBI's other priorities. The central bank has intervened heavily to support the rupee through a difficult year marked by an oil price shock and capital outflows. With currency stability at the top of its agenda, adding to gold holdings appears to have taken a back seat, even as it continues to secure the bullion it already owns.

news.title: Gold's downside looks limited because the dollar has already done most of its work, CBA says
body: If CBA is right, gold traders should be watching the dollar index and US real yields more closely than geopolitical headlines. The December Fed decision is the near-term test. A hike that is already expected, with no hawkish surprise in the guidance, could let the dollar plateau and help gold stabilise. A signal that more hikes are coming would push real yields higher and test the lower end of CBA's range. Gold's renewed inverse link to the dollar also means moves in dollar-yen and euro-dollar may give an early read on bullion. With only weeks until year-end, CBA's range doubles as a near-term trading band.

CBA says gold has gone back to trading off the dollar and real yields rather than haven demand, and with the dollar already close to the bank's forecast peak, it sees limited downside and a year-end range of $3,500 to $3,700.

The dollar is set to be the main force behind gold prices in the coming months, according to Commonwealth Bank of Australia. The bank argues that the downside for the metal now looks limited, because the greenback is already close to its expected peak.

CBA expects gold to end the year at around $3,500 to $3,700 an ounce, close to where the metal has been trading this week after a steep selloff. The bank's case rests on a shift in what is driving bullion. Earlier in the cycle, the "sell America" trade and bets on a weakening, debased dollar pushed investors towards gold as a structural haven. Those trades are now giving way to more traditional relationships, CBA said, in particular gold's tendency to move in the opposite direction to the dollar and to US 10-year real Treasury yields. As a result, structural safe-haven demand has become a less important support for the metal.

That puts the dollar's trajectory at the centre of the outlook. The greenback has risen faster than CBA expected and is now close to the peak the bank had forecast for the middle of 2027. If most of the dollar's rally is already done, the main headwind for gold may be close to its maximum strength. In CBA's view, that suggests the risk of further steep losses in gold is limited.

The call fits the broader picture of gold's slide this year. The metal has fallen sharply as a stronger dollar, rising expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes and selling in stock markets pushed investors to raise cash. Higher real yields increase the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and that relationship appears to be reasserting itself.

CBA's view sits at the more constructive end of a divided field. HSBC warned this week that continued equity weakness could push gold through major support at $3,400, and said it is too early to call an end to the slide. Saxo's Ole Hansen, by contrast, pointed to signs of selling exhaustion and set out a path towards around $3,700 if gold can close above roughly $3,590.

The risks to CBA's view run through the same channel. A dollar that overshoots the bank's forecast peak, or a further rise in real yields if the Fed hikes more aggressively than expected, would leave gold vulnerable. On the other hand, any sign that the dollar has topped out would strengthen the case that the worst of gold's decline is over.

news.title: Tokyo core inflation hits 16-month high of 2.9%, firming the case for a December BoJ hike
body: The data keeps a December hike as the base case, which should limit any yen weakness. With the yen near 160 per dollar, however, a 25 basis point move that is already widely expected may do little on its own. The bigger driver for the currency is likely to be any signal that the BoJ will speed up its pace of hikes, as board member Naoki Tamura has urged. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields remain sensitive to that guidance. Stock market instability tied to AI and chips is the main risk to the hike call, so a sharp drop in Japanese equities would quickly cut the odds of a December move.

Tokyo core inflation has climbed to its fastest pace in 16 months, strengthening the case for a December BoJ hike, though a slight easing in the bank's preferred trend gauge suggests energy did much of the lifting.

Core inflation in Tokyo climbed to its highest in 16 months in November, keeping price growth well above the Bank of Japan's 2% target and reinforcing expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates next month.

Core consumer prices in the capital, which include fuel but exclude fresh food, rose 2.9% from a year earlier, according to data reported by Reuters on Friday. That was up from 2.6% in October and the fastest annual pace since July 2025, although it fell just short of the 3.0% median forecast. Core inflation has now held above the BoJ's target for three consecutive months.

The end of government utility subsidies accounted for part of the jump, but the increases were broad-based, with prices rising for food, daily necessities and hotel stays. One economist expects core inflation to keep accelerating as higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict feed through into other prices.

The picture is a little softer underneath. A measure that strips out both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches closely as a gauge of trend inflation, eased slightly to 2.5% from 2.6% in October. That leaves underlying inflation comfortably above target, but suggests energy did much of the heavy lifting in the core rise.

Tokyo figures are widely seen as a leading indicator for the nationwide data. Those are due on the morning of December 18 in Tokyo, the final day of the BoJ's two-day policy meeting. That timing makes Friday's release one of the last major inflation readings that policymakers and markets can fully weigh before the decision.

Markets widely expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from 1.25% at that meeting. The bank has already moved faster than in previous years, hiking in June and again in September, compared with roughly two hikes a year in 2024 and 2025. In October it held rates, but said underlying inflation had roughly reached its 2% target and signalled readiness to keep tightening. A majority of economists in a Reuters poll expect a December hike followed by another by the end of March, with many seeing rates peaking at around 1.75% or 2.0%.
Hawkish board member Naoki Tamura added to the pressure on Thursday, saying the bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by speeding up its pace of hikes.

The main risk to a December move comes from markets. The same economist said the BoJ could hold off if instability linked to worries over AI and the chip sector persists, though a hike next month remains the baseline.

news.title: HSBC flags $3,400 as gold's next big test and says it is too early to call a bottom
body: Gold is trading as a risk asset rather than a haven, so equity markets have become the key driver. Another leg lower in stocks would raise the chance of a test of $3,400, while a stabilisation would ease the forced selling. Silver and platinum group metals face an extra layer of risk from tariffs that could hit the industries using them, even though HSBC still expects silver to be in deficit. US tariff announcements are worth watching, especially any aimed at Mexico or Canada, which HSBC sees as the exception that could lift silver. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December, a softer turn in US data is the most likely trigger for relief.
HSBC sees gold's fortunes tied to a weak stock market, with $3,400 the next major support at risk, and warns that proposed tariffs could hurt silver and platinum group metals more than gold itself.

HSBC says it is too early to call an end to gold's slide, warning that further weakness in stock markets could push the metal through its next major support at $3,400 an ounce. The bank also sees limits to how far the selloff can run.

The warning, carried by Reuters on Thursday, adds to the cautious camp as gold struggles to find a floor. HSBC's chief precious metals analyst, James Steel, tied the risk directly to equities. Gold traded near $3,570 on Thursday in thin holiday conditions, after slipping below $3,500 midweek to its lowest in more than a year. The link to stocks reflects the forced selling behind the metal's fall this year: investors raising cash to cover equity losses have been selling what they can, including gold.

The $3,400 level carries extra weight in Steel's analysis. He has previously described it as roughly the inflation-adjusted equivalent of gold's old record high, a level the metal broke above in 2025. A sustained move back below it would undo a milestone that helped define gold's bull run.

HSBC also turned to trade policy. Trade distortions have traditionally been positive for gold, the bank said, but proposed new US tariffs could weigh on industries that use large amounts of silver and platinum group metals. That puts the industrial side of the precious metals complex more at risk than gold itself.

On silver, HSBC still projects a market deficit this year, even as demand from high-tech and industrial users declines. It does not expect fresh tariffs on their own to push silver prices higher, unless they are aimed at Mexico and Canada, both important suppliers of silver to the US.

HSBC's view adds to a growing debate over whether gold has bottomed. TD Securities' head of commodity strategy also said on Thursday that it is likely too early to call a low in gold and the wider precious metals complex. Others see the selloff as overdone. Saxo's Ole Hansen pointed this week to signs of selling exhaustion, stretched positioning and a strong seasonal record over December and January. He stressed, though, that a lasting recovery depends on the dollar and rate expectations easing.

For now, markets are pricing a high chance of another Federal Reserve rate hike in December, which continues to weigh on a metal that pays no yield. Until that pressure eases or stocks stabilise, $3,400 is likely to remain the level traders watch.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6604 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
body: The views point to a widening gap in how investors treat the AI trade. Hyperscaler stocks and investment-grade bonds look the most defensible, given their strong balance sheets and cash flows outside AI. Neocloud equity and high-yield credit carry the most risk if utilisation disappoints. Goldman's credit team expects the high-yield market for AI deals to split more sharply, with investors favouring top-tier developers and projects backed by solid contracts. Chipmakers and memory suppliers ultimately depend on the same thing as the neoclouds: evidence that companies using AI are earning a return. The next earnings round's commentary on returns on capital is likely to move the whole complex.

Goldman's analysis suggests the tech giants can comfortably earn a return on their AI build-out, but the neoclouds renting out GPU capacity are exposed if corporate customers keep failing to turn AI spending into profit.

Is the artificial intelligence spending boom built to last? Goldman Sachs put that question to two people who see the cycle from very different vantage points, and their answers point the same way. The biggest technology companies are well placed to ride out a slowdown. The risk is concentrated among newer, more heavily indebted players further down the chain.

Goldman's lead US internet analyst, Eric Sheridan, argued in the bank's November Top of Mind report that the six largest US hyperscalers can "very easily" earn a return on invested capital of 15% or more on their AI spending. Their revenue backlogs are much larger than two or three years ago, and some companies have said about half of those backlogs will turn into revenue within two years. On Goldman's estimates, the hyperscalers would not need anywhere near all of that backlog to convert to reach the 15% mark. Sheridan pointed to the latest earnings round, in which several of the big names gave detailed return figures and their shares rallied, as evidence that the payoff is starting to show.

He described the market's current doubts as understandable, rather than either warranted or overblown. Every computing cycle he has covered, from desktop to mobile to cloud, has gone through a phase of disillusionment once spending runs ahead of visible returns. Investors, he said, want returns within months on a build-out that typically plays out over five to eight years.

Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of Social Capital, invests across AI chips, power and software. He is more worried about the neoclouds, the specialist firms that rent out GPU capacity. He compares them to a bank in reverse: their revenue is short-term and uncertain, while their obligations for chips, power and data centres are long-dated and fixed. Like airlines, they need to keep their capacity busy to make money. He puts the break-even point at roughly 70% to 75% utilisation, with profits only coming above that. Yearly chip upgrades and more efficient AI models make the arithmetic harder.

His central concern is that big companies are not yet earning a meaningful return on their AI spending. Projects are hard to implement, staff are often wary, and productivity gains tend to get lost elsewhere in the business, so few firms can point to AI as a source of earnings growth. If that remains the case, demand for computing power may not grow fast enough to fill the capacity being built.

Goldman's analysts put the hurdle in numbers. For the hyperscalers to earn a 15% return on their 2026 and 2027 investment, they would need to generate around $1.4 trillion in cumulative revenue over 2028 to 2030, roughly $500 billion a year. Sheridan sees three things that could stall the cycle: weaker demand, a disruption in access to capital, or a shortage of power, which cannot be scaled up as fast as land, buildings or chips. For now, he sees demand gaining momentum rather than fading.

Both expect the cycle to produce winners and losers. Palihapitiya expects a bump in the road at some point, much like the internet build-out two decades ago, which ultimately proved right but got the timing wrong. Neoclouds that own their power and land should hold up better than those that simply lease capacity.
